title: Client steering hints and orchestration scratchpad
content:
Status: sketch / working notes
Owner: Aisha Patel (platform eng) — working through ideas for combining client-side hints with centralized orchestration to improve locality and graceful failover across regions.

Goal summary
- Reduce tail latency and cross-region hairpins by allowing authoritative control-plane decisions while leveraging lightweight client-side hints where available.
- Provide a simple, backward-compatible mechanism to bias routing (GeoDNS/Anycast) without losing global capacity or creating undetectable blackholes during capacity changes.
- Minimize operational blast radius during regional failures and support soft handoffs for long-lived sessions.

Context and motivation
We currently operate multi-region endpoints with a mix of Anycast for edge ingress and regional egress endpoints controlled by GeoDNS. Problems we keep seeing:
- DNS TTLs and client caches make rapid failover noisy or slow.
- Pure Anycast reduces DNS fiddling but makes capacity-aware routing harder (hard to direct traffic away from saturated region).
- Customers with strict latency SLOs want stronger locality preference (not just proximity), e.g., prefer region with cheaper access path even if slightly farther.
- Long-lived websocket/streaming sessions need soft handoffs to avoid disconnects on failover.

Core idea (hybrid steering model)
1) Control plane publishes compact per-region steering tokens and preference vectors as short-lived JSON blobs (signed): region_bias_v1. Each token includes region id, capacity score, epoch, and a short fingerprint.
2) Edge / Anycast gateways periodically fetch these tokens and advertise BGP communities or set local routing weights internally.
3) Clients that are steering-aware (SDKs, sidecars, or first-party mobile apps) can include a client_hint header: X-RW-Region-Hint: <signed-token-id> or X-RW-Prefer-Regions: eu-west-1,us-west-2;weight=0.8
4) Ingress gateways combine client hints with local telemetry and policy to select the target region. A simple ranked choice algorithm: prefer client hints if token epoch within TTL and region capacity > threshold; otherwise fall back to control-plane preference list.

Why this is different from strict GeoDNS or Anycast
- GeoDNS tries to map client IP->region at resolution time; caches cause lag. The hybrid model keeps DNS for coarse locality but uses lightweight runtime hints for fast adjustments.
- Anycast handles hairpinning and shortest-path routing but doesn’t let us shift traffic away from an overwhelmed region. Adding region tokens to gateways enables admission control without changing global BGP.

Gateway selection heuristics (sketch)
Inputs: client_hint (optional), client_ip_geo, local_probe_score, regional_capacity_score, policy_tier (enterprise vs default), request_type (streaming|rpc|embed), sticky_affinity_token (optional).
Algorithm (pseudocode prose):
- If sticky_affinity_token present and token valid -> route to token.region unless capacity < 20% -> attempt soft handoff (see below).
- Else if client_hint present and signed and epoch newer than (now - 30s) and region capacity > 50% -> route to hinted region with probability p = min(1.0, capacity_score * hint_weight).
- Else consult local preference vector from control plane; apply weighted randomization so a noisy threshold doesn't flip 100% of requests; use soft ramp (10%-100% over 30s) when shifting.

Soft handoffs for long-lived sessions
- When a region is being drained/evicted, issue a handoff token with a TTL (e.g., 300s) and a handoff endpoint list.
- Gateway marks session as draining and returns a short 202+X-RW-Handoff header to client library. Client library attempts parallel establish to primary+secondary for short window and then switches once new connection stable.
- Server-side: maintain session state replication or sticky token exchange for rehydrate on failover. If session state isn't available, perform graceful degrade and return structured error indicating partial progress.

Control plane responsibilities and APIs (notes)
- Publish region metrics: effective concurrency, p50/p99 egress latency, health, capacity units available. These are aggregated and rolled up into a compact region preference vector (signed).
- Steering API: POST /v2/steering/publish {policy_id, region_weights[], epoch, signature}. Workers fetch every 5s with backoff.
- Exposure: customers can set preference overrides (e.g., legal region limits) which control-plane validates and injects into region_weights with an override flag.
- Telemetry loop: gateways emit sampled request traces, admission drops, and probe results. Control plane re-evaluates weights every 10s (tunable).

Interaction with DNS and TTLs
- Keep authoritative DNS TTLs for region endpoints moderately long (60s–300s) to avoid excessive global churn, but implement runtime steering so we don't rely on DNS for immediate failover.
- Use low TTL for special failover record (e.g., failover.<service>) if customer opts-in to faster DNS-driven fallback. Default behavior: rely on gateway tokens + Anycast for quickness, DNS for coarse fallback.
- Consider EDNS-client-subnet privacy: do not require ECS for steering-aware clients — client_hint is preferred because ECS leaks client netblock to DNS provider which can be undesirable.

Anycast + per-region ejection
- Anycast remains primary for ingress. When region overloaded, gateways locally reject or shed with structured 429 and handoff suggestion header; they do NOT silently drop to avoid user-observable blackholes.
- Rather than withdraw BGP for an entire POP, prefer local weight adjustment and let the control plane coordinate gradual ejection (percent of sessions rerouted over mins).

Telemetry, invariants, and safety checks
- Control plane must never direct > 95% of global traffic to any single region unless explicit override (prevents cascading failures).
- Rollout experiments: support canary steering policies for small subset of customers with forced local pref to test steering logic without global impact.
- Alerting: rapid capacity change (>30% drop in available units in 60s) triggers automated gradual failover plan + paging for on-call.

Operational runbook fragments (what on-call does)
- Detect: p99 egress rises in region -> look at capacity score and queue depth; check gateway-heavy rejection headers.
- Mitigate: if transient, increase local admission control threshold; if sustained, publish a drain epoch and initiate soft handoff tokens.
- Escalate: if drain fails or inter-region replication broken, flip DNS failover for impacted customers (use low-TTL failover record) and open incident.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- How much cryptographic signing do we need on tokens? HMAC vs short-lived JWTs? Signing introduces CPU overhead on gateways.
- TTL choices: shorter TTLs help failover but increase global DNS QPS and cost. Balance via hybrid approach.
- SDK adoption: steering benefits only when client libs adopt headers. How much to prioritize server-side-only fallback?
- Data residency: how to guarantee traffic never leaves approved regions when using Anycast? Need strict ingress gating at gateway.

Experiment ideas (quick A/B)
- Small cohort of clients get client_hint enabled; measure p50/p99 improvement and failure modes.
- Test soft handoff by simulating capacity degradation and measuring session continuity with sidecar vs without.

Immediate TODOs
- Draft minimal token format and signing (Aisha)
- Spike: implement gateway ingest logic for token+hint selection (Diego)
- Instrument: add telemetry fields for hint-used, token-epoch, chosen-region (Liam)
- Run tabletop for soft-handoff incident playbook (platform on-call + SRE)

Notes to self
- Keep control-plane decisions auditable and replayable (store epoch history for 72h).
- Make policy deterministic given same inputs (for easier debugging) but allow stochastic weighted choices for load smoothing.

References / inspiration
- Hybrid steering notes from external CDN architectures (edge tokens + control-plane steering)
- Internal: region-steering-notes-2024 (confluence) and Anycast-locality-playbook (archived)

End of scratchpad.
